Hexagonal Architecture Simplified Part 1: From Messy MVC to Hexagonal Architecture
Introduction - Why Architecture Matters
If you’ve ever worked on a backend, you know the sinking feeling: you need to add a small feature, but changing one line triggers a cascade of bugs. Controllers are packed with business logic, database queries are scattered everywhere, and external API calls are tangled into the same mess. It works… for now. But as the system grows, it quickly becomes brittle, hard to maintain, and a nightmare to test.
This is exactly the problem Hexagonal Architecture is designed to solve (or at least, intends to). By creating clear boundaries around your core domain, it separates business logic from databases, frameworks, and external systems. The result is code that is clean, testable, flexible, and easier to evolve, even as new requirements or integrations appear.
In this two-part series, we’ll take a simple Shipment Tracking System and transform it step by step:
Part 1: Refactor a messy multi-layer backend into a single hexagon with ports, adapters, and a clean domain.
Part 2: Expand to multiple collaborating hexagons, showing how different parts of the system interact.
By the end of this first part, you’ll see how even small structural changes can turn a tangled, fragile backend into a solid foundation, ready for scaling, domain modeling, and reliable testing in the later stages of the series.
The Messy Starting Point: Multi-Layer Shipment Tracking System
Imagine a shipment tracking system built with a standard multi-layer architecture: controllers, services, and database entities. At first glance, it seems well-structured - each layer has its responsibility, right? But take a closer look, and you’ll see the reality is a little messier. Business logic, persistence, and external API calls are all tangled together, creating a system that’s hard to maintain, test, or extend.
Here’s a simplified example in TypeScript:
// Controller app.post("/shipments", async (req, res) => { const shipmentData = req.body; const shipmentService = new ShipmentService(); const shipment = await shipmentService.createShipment(shipmentData); res.send(shipment); });
// Service class ShipmentService { async createShipment(data: ShipmentData) { // Save shipment to database const shipment = new ShipmentEntity(data); await shipment.save(); // Call external tracking API through static handler const gpsData = await ApiHandler.callApi(`https://gps-api.com/${shipment.id}`); // Combine data and return return { ...shipment, gps: gpsData }; } }
// Database Entity (example with ORM) class ShipmentEntity { constructor(private data: ShipmentData) {} async save() { // Simulate DB save console.log("Saved to DB:", this.data); } } // Generic API Call Handler class ApiHandler { static async callApi(url: string): Promise { // Simulate external API call console.log("Calling API:", url); return { lat: 40.7128, lng: -74.0060 }; // Example GPS coordinates } }
What’s Going Wrong Here?
Even though we’ve separated layers, the system still has several hidden problems:
1.
Business logic leaks across layers: The service handles database persistence, API calls, and combines results for the response.
2.
Tightly coupled to infrastructure: The service knows about the database entity and the static API handler.
3.
Hard to test: Testing ShipmentService requires mocking both the database and the API.
4.
Difficult to scale or extend: Adding new adapters or integrations means modifying the service logic, risking unintended side effects.
Now let us ask a question. What can go wrong if we want to add more complex scenarios??
1. When Scaling Layers Starts to Crack
At first glance, a multi-layer architecture looks perfectly fine - controllers handle HTTP requests, services manage logic, repositories talk to the database, and everything flows neatly downward. It feels structured, logical, and easy to reason about.
But as the system grows - new features, more APIs, additional integrations - those layers start to work against you. Every dependency in this setup points outward, from business logic toward infrastructure. Your core domain logic, which should be the most stable part of your system, ends up depending on the database, the ORM, or external services.
And here’s where it hurts: one small schema change or API update can ripple through the entire stack - repositories, services, controllers, and even tests. You’re no longer building on a solid foundation; you’re building on top of everything that can change tomorrow.
2. When the Core Domain Isn’t Really at the Core
As the architecture expands, business logic often starts mixing with infrastructure details. Repositories begin to leak SQL queries or ORM-specific behavior into the service layer. Before long, your so-called “core domain” becomes aware of caching strategies, HTTP calls, or API response formats.
This means the domain logic isn’t really isolated anymore. Every change in the database or integration affects business rules that should have been untouched. Testing becomes harder too - you can’t test a service without spinning up the database or mocking complex dependencies. The clean separation you started with slowly blurs until the system becomes a tangled web of hidden dependencies.
3. When Change Becomes a Chain Reaction
Now imagine the business decides to switch from PostgreSQL to MongoDB. In theory, it’s just an infrastructure change. But in a multi-layer system, it doesn’t stop there. Repository methods tied to SQL logic must change, services depending on query behavior break, and even controllers might need adjustments to fit new data shapes.
The result is a chain reaction - a small infrastructure tweak forces modifications across multiple layers. Maintenance becomes risky, refactoring slows down, and each change starts to feel like defusing a bomb. What seemed like a scalable architecture on day one turns into a system where everything depends on everything else.
Core Principles of Hexagonal Architecture
Before we start untangling our messy shipment tracking system, it’s worth stepping back and understanding what Hexagonal Architecture really means and why it’s so powerful. At its core, Hexagonal Architecture (also known as the Ports and Adapters pattern) is about keeping your business logic independent from the outside world. It’s like building a small fortress around your core domain, with carefully designed gates that let information in and out - but never allow chaos to leak inside.
The Heart of the Hexagon: The Domain
At the center of every hexagonal system lives the Domain - the core of your business logic. This is where your real value resides: entities, rules, and use cases that define what your system does, not how it’s done. The domain doesn’t know or care about databases, APIs, or frameworks. It just knows the rules of your business.
For our shipment tracking system, that domain might include:
•
The logic for creating and updating shipments.
•
Rules for when a shipment can be marked as in transit or delivered.
•
Business decisions about what happens if tracking data is missing.
Everything else - the database, the API calls, the message queues - lives outside the hexagon.
Ports: The Gateways of Communication
Think of the domain as a secure fortress that holds your core business logic and the Ports as the gates that control how anyone outside can talk to it. Ports define what kind of conversations are allowed, without revealing any details of what goes on inside the walls.
In practical terms, a Port is an interface - a contract that tells the outside world, “Here’s what I can do,” without explaining how it’s done. For instance, a port might say: “Here’s how you can save a shipment,” or “Here’s how you can request tracking data.”
These contracts live within the domain layer itself, because they describe the needs and capabilities of the business logic. But their implementations - like the actual database call or API request - live elsewhere, outside the domain.
In short, Ports describe the intent of communication, not its implementation. And in the next section, we’ll see who actually opens those gates and handles that communication - the Adapters.
This clean separation ensures that the domain logic stays focused on business rules, while the technical details of communication remain flexible and replaceable.
Adapters: The Outer Shell
If Ports define what conversations the domain can have, then Adapters are the ones who actually speak those conversations in the language of the outside world.
Adapters live outside the hexagon, at the edges of your system. Their job is to handle everything that’s specific to your infrastructure - making HTTP calls, writing to databases, consuming events, or exposing REST endpoints.
There are generally two types of adapters:
•
Inbound Adapters: These are the entry points that bring requests into your domain. Examples include API controllers, message consumers, or CLI commands.
•
Outbound Adapters: These let your domain talk outward to other systems, such as repositories that save data to a database, or clients that call external APIs.
You can think of adapters as translators standing at the border of your system. They understand the world’s languages - HTTP, SQL, JSON, or gRPC - and convert them into the clean, business-oriented language of your domain.
This separation means your core logic never needs to know how data is stored or fetched; it simply communicates through Ports, while Adapters handle the rest.
Why the Hexagon Shape?
The hexagon isn’t literal - it’s symbolic. It represents the idea of symmetry: the domain can interact with any number of external systems equally, through well-defined ports and adapters. It doesn’t matter if data comes from a database, a web API, a CLI command, or a test script, they all connect through the same consistent boundaries.

How It Changes the Way You Think
In a traditional layered or MVC architecture, your business logic often sits in the middle - but everything around it can reach in and change it. In a hexagonal architecture, the domain becomes untouchable. Infrastructure depends on the domain - not the other way around.
This single inversion of dependency changes everything:
•
Code becomes testable because the domain doesn’t rely on real databases or APIs.
•
Code becomes maintainable because external systems can change without breaking your core.
•
Code becomes adaptable because you can swap out adapters (say, from a REST API to a message queue) without rewriting business logic.
Now, let’s circle back to the shipment system we started with. We already know it has a solid core of business logic - we’re just missing a clean structure to protect it. That’s exactly where our new understanding of Ports and Adapters comes in.
By refactoring the existing controllers, services, and entities, we can start shaping them into a self-contained hexagon. The domain will sit safely at the center, while the ports define how it communicates with the outside world. The adapters - will live around the edges, handling all the external details like APIs and databases.
In the next section, we’ll walk through this transformation step by step. You’ll see how our messy, layered system turns into a clean, testable architecture - both in code and in structure.
Step-by-Step Refactoring: Extracting the Domain, Ports, and Adapters
Now that we understand the core idea behind Hexagonal Architecture - keeping our business logic at the center and isolating it from the outside world - let’s get our hands dirty.
We’ll take our messy shipment tracking system and refactor it into a clean, single hexagon. Along the way, you’ll see how our tangled dependencies gradually transform into a clear, maintainable structure.
Step 1: Where We Started
Our multi-layered system looked neat on paper - controllers, services, and entities, but everything was tightly coupled. The service directly saved data to the database and made an API call, mixing business logic with infrastructure.
Symptoms:
•
The domain logic can’t be tested in isolation.
•
The service depends on infrastructure (DB, API).
•
Any change in the DB or external API ripples through the core logic.
Step 2: Finding the Core Domain
Let’s start by extracting the business logic - the part that actually defines what our system does.
At the heart of it, creating a shipment means:
1.
Creating a Shipment entity.
2.
Saving it somewhere.
3.
Asking a tracking service for GPS data.
That’s the pure domain flow. So let’s isolate that inside a dedicated domain service.
// domain/ShipmentService.ts import { Shipment } from "./Shipment"; import { ShipmentRepository } from "../ports/ShipmentRepository"; import { TrackingService } from "../ports/TrackingService"; export class ShipmentService { constructor( private shipmentRepo: ShipmentRepository, private trackingService: TrackingService ) {} async createShipment(data: ShipmentData) { const shipment = new Shipment(data); await this.shipmentRepo.save(shipment); const gpsData = await this.trackingService.trackShipment(shipment.id); return { ...shipment, gps: gpsData }; } }
Step 3: Define the Ports
Now, instead of directly calling the database or API, our domain depends on abstractions - the ports. Let’s add them.
// ports/ShipmentRepository.ts import { Shipment } from "../domain/Shipment"; export interface ShipmentRepository { save(shipment: Shipment): Promise; }
// ports/TrackingService.ts export interface TrackingService { trackShipment(id: string): Promise; }
These ports define “what” the domain needs - but not “how it’s done”. It is done through these contracts (Interfaces). That’s the key: our domain is now free of infrastructure details.
Step 4: Add Adapters
The adapters sit on the outside of the hexagon and implement those ports. They contain the infrastructure logic - database operations, HTTP calls, etc. Here we are adding two adapters - one for each port that we created earlier.
// adapters/DatabaseShipmentRepository.ts import { ShipmentRepository } from "../ports/ShipmentRepository"; import { Shipment } from "../domain/Shipment"; export class DatabaseShipmentRepository implements ShipmentRepository { async save(shipment: Shipment): Promise { console.log("Saving to DB:", shipment); // ORM logic would go here in a real app } }
// adapters/ExternalTrackingAdapter.ts import { TrackingService } from "../ports/TrackingService"; export class ExternalTrackingAdapter implements TrackingService { async trackShipment(id: string): Promise { console.log("Calling external tracking API for:", id); return { lat: 51.5074456, lng: -0.1277653 }; } }
Step 5: Wire It All Together
Finally, our controller (or inbound adapter) wires everything up - connecting the domain to the real world.
// app.ts const shipmentRepo = new DatabaseShipmentRepository(); const trackingService = new ExternalTrackingAdapter(); const shipmentService = new ShipmentService(shipmentRepo, trackingService); app.post("/shipments", async (req, res) => { const shipmentData = req.body; const shipment = await shipmentService.createShipment(shipmentData); res.send(shipment); });
After Refactoring: One Clean Hexagon
Here’s what our system looks like now:
In our example, the ShipmentService itself acts as the inbound port - the main entry point to the domain. We haven’t created a separate ShipmentPort interface yet, and that’s completely fine at this stage.
In Hexagonal Architecture, the goal is to keep the domain independent from the outside world, not to force every boundary into a separate interface right away.
We can always extract a formal inbound port later, especially if we need multiple adapters (like REST, GraphQL, or gRPC) calling the same use case. For now, we are keeping it this way to make it easier to understand.
What We’ve Gained after refactor
•
Isolation: The core domain doesn’t depend on any framework, database, or API.
•
Flexibility: We can replace the database adapter or the tracking adapter without changing business logic.
•
Testability: We can test the domain using mocks for ports - no need for real databases or API calls.
•
Clarity: Each layer now has a clear purpose: the domain defines the “what”, adapters handle the “how”.
The business rules are now the center of gravity - not the infrastructure.
Wrapping Up: From Code Cleanup to Architectural Clarity
We started this journey with a simple goal - to make sense of a messy shipment-tracking system. At first, it looked fine: a controller, a service, a database entity, and an API call. But as we dug deeper, we saw how tightly everything was glued together. Every change in one place risked breaking another.
Then, we zoomed out and looked at the bigger picture - Hexagonal Architecture. We learned that at the heart of every system lies its domain, and everything else should orbit around it. We introduced ports and adapters as the clean boundaries that protect the domain from the chaos of the outside world.
Finally, we rolled up our sleeves and refactored our code - step by step - into our first hexagon. Now, our shipment logic lives peacefully at the center, shielded from databases, APIs, and frameworks.
At this point we have a solid foundation - one hexagon that’s ready to grow into a true architectural system.
This isn’t just refactoring; it’s a change in how we think about software. It’s moving from “where do I put this code?” to “who should own this responsibility?”
Closing Thought
Hexagonal Architecture isn’t just about diagrams or folder structures - it’s about discipline. It’s also about building systems that can stand the test of change. Because in the end, great software isn’t defined by how it looks when it’s built - it’s defined by how gracefully it adapts when everything around it changes.
